traveler: Kublai Khan (Khubilai, Setsen Khan, Emperor Shizu of Yuan)
title: From the Kerulen to the Taiye Lake: the Grandson Who Built a Capital and Lost the Steppe
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Kerulen River valley, the birth of Tolui's second son
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the day 23 September is given by Wikipedia and by the standard biographies, though some sources give only the year. The birthplace is not recorded in any primary source and the Kerulen heartland is inferred from Tolui's appanage.
stops.campa: On the grass of the Kerulen, in the appanage of Tolui, Sorghaghtani Beki bears her second son and he is named Kublai. His grandfather is alive and campaigning in north China. The mother is a Kerait princess and a Nestorian Christian who reads her sons' futures the way other women read weather; she will raise four and see three of them made Great Khan. No chronicle records the tent, the hour, or the ground. The steppe keeps no addresses, and the empire that will later need a birthplace for him has to guess at one.
suggested_refs: The Kerulen river heartland of the Borjigin appanage, birth region inferred from Tolui's holdings
sources: Morris Rossabi, Khubilai Khan: His Life and Times

stops.name: Ili River valley, the first hunt
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the year 1224 is standard but the month is unrecorded and defaults to January. The episode survives only through Rashid al-Din and later chronicles written for the dynasty the boy founded.
stops.campa: At nine the boy rides out with Genghis Khan above the Ili and kills a rabbit and a goat. His grandfather smears the fat of the kill on Kublai's thumb, the rite by which a Mongol child is counted a hunter. Rashid al-Din adds that the old Khan hears the boy speak and calls his words full of wisdom. The men who write this down are writing for a dynasty already founded, and the scene reads as prophecy because everyone reading it knows what the boy became. It is the only story of his childhood anyone thought worth keeping.
suggested_refs: Rashid al-Din's account of the thumb-anointing rite at the first kill

stops.name: Liupanshan, the death of the grandfather
stops.date_confidence: attested; the date 18 August 1227 is the one carried in the atlas by the genghis_khan journey. Wikipedia's 'Kublai Khan' calls Kublai twelve at his grandfather's death; born 23 September 1215, he is eleven and turns twelve the following month.
stops.campa: In the Liupan mountains Genghis Khan dies on campaign against the Tangut, and the world he assembled passes to his sons. Kublai is eleven, a month short of twelve, and stands nowhere near the succession: he is the second son of the fourth son, with uncles and cousins ahead of him in every reckoning. The atlas already carries genghis_khan to this mountain. No throne comes to the grandson here. What he takes from it is a method, and the memory of a rite performed on his thumb three years earlier on the Ili.
suggested_refs: genghis_khan.journey.json, stop at Liupanshan, 18 August 1227

stops.name: Xingzhou, ten thousand households in Hebei
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the Yuan Shi and in Wikipedia; no month recorded, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: After the Jin dynasty falls, Ogedei grants the young prince an estate in Hebei of ten thousand households. The estate is the first sedentary ground Kublai governs, and the first time he answers for people who plough. Mongol practice is to tax such districts through farmers of revenue and let the countryside empty; Kublai's Chinese and Khitan advisers persuade him to do the opposite, and households that had fled begin to return. His father Tolui has been dead four years. The prince is twenty-one and has found the argument of his life.
suggested_refs: The Xingzhou appanage records summarized in the Yuan Shi
sources: Yuan Shi (History of Yuan), cited in Morris Rossabi, Khubilai Khan

stops.name: Karakorum, the monk Haiyun and the birth of an heir
stops.date_confidence: the Haiyun meeting is dated 1242 by the Yuan Shi and Wikipedia. Wikipedia's 'Kublai Khan' puts Zhenjin's birth in the same year; Wikipedia's 'Zhenjin' gives 8 July 1243. The contradiction is left standing here.
stops.campa: At the Mongol capital Kublai receives the Chan Buddhist master Haiyun and asks him what Buddhism is for. Taoists, Nestorians, Muslims and Tibetan lamas will follow Haiyun to that tent in turn, each convinced they are converting him and none of them wrong enough to leave. Haiyun names the prince's son, born within a year: Zhenjin, True Gold, a Chinese name for a Mongol heir. The sources disagree on whether the boy is born in 1242 or on 8 July 1243, and no one has reconciled them.
suggested_refs: The Yuan Shi record of the Haiyun audience; Wikipedia, 'Zhenjin'

stops.name: Jingzhao, the viceroy and the auditors
stops.date_confidence: appointment attested for 1251; no month given. The audit of Kublai's administration and its 142 regulatory breaches is dated 1257 by Wikipedia and belongs to the end of this posting.
stops.campa: His brother Mongke becomes Great Khan and gives Kublai the Chinese territories to govern. He bases himself near Xi'an, staffs his secretariat with Chinese and Khitan scholars, restores land to cultivation and taxes it in grain rather than farming it out. By 1257 the court has noticed: Mongke sends tax inspectors north, they find one hundred and forty-two breaches of regulation among Kublai's administrators, and the brother who governs too well in the Chinese manner is stripped of his commands. He submits without arguing, and waits.
suggested_refs: The 1257 audit of the northern secretariat, Yuan Shi

stops.name: Jinsha River at Shigu, the crossing on inflated skins
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the month is not fixed in the reachable sources and October is the campaigning season implied by the march. The pin is placed on the First Bend of the Yangtze at Shigu.
stops.campa: Ordered south against Yunnan, Kublai brings his column to the great bend of the Jinsha, where the Yangtze turns back on itself under the mountains. The army crosses by night on rafts buoyed with inflated hides and routs the Dali force waiting on the far bank. It is his first independent command. The road into the Dali kingdom opens behind the crossing, and with it the long southwestern flank that will later let Yuan armies reach Burma, Champa and the Red River delta without ever passing the Song.
suggested_refs: The First Bend of the Yangtze at Shigu, Yulong County, Lijiang

stops.name: Dali, the kingdom taken and the lama acquired
stops.date_confidence: the fall of Dali city is attested for 1253; the month is not fixed. Resistance continues to about 1256, and King Duan Xingzhi flees to Shanchan rather than surrendering with the city.
stops.campa: Dali city falls, and the three-century Bai kingdom under the Cangshan mountains passes to the Mongols. King Duan Xingzhi escapes to Shanchan and the war drags two more years before Yunnan is fully absorbed. Kublai spares the city on his advisers' urging rather than putting it to the customary sack. Out of this campaign he takes into his household the young Tibetan monk Drogon Chogyal Phagpa, who will design him an alphabet, crown him a Buddhist king, and give the Yuan its state religion.
suggested_refs: The Sakya lineage records of Phagpa's entry into Kublai's entourage

stops.name: Thang Long, the first burning
stops.date_confidence: attested for early 1258; the campaign is conducted by Uriyangkhadai out of the Dali command Kublai established, not by Kublai in person.
stops.campa: The general Uriyangkhadai, operating from the Yunnan command Kublai built, marches down the Red River and takes the Dai Viet capital. The Tran court withdraws, the Mongols hold the city, the climate and the supply lines do the rest, and within weeks the invaders pull back north. It is the first of three Mongol descents on Vietnam across Kublai's lifetime and the shortest. Each of the three will end the same way: a capital entered, a court that refuses to be in it, and an army retreating up the river it came down.
suggested_refs: Dai Viet Su Ky Toan Thu, account of the 1258 occupation of Thang Long
sources: Dai Viet Su Ky Toan Thu

stops.name: Diaoyu Fortress, the Great Khan dies on the cliff
stops.date_confidence: attested; 11 August 1259 per Wikipedia, 'Mongke Khan'. The pin sits on Diaoyu Mountain just east of Hechuan.
stops.campa: Mongke Khan dies at the siege of the cliff fortress of Diaoyucheng in Sichuan, a rock the Mongols have failed to take for months. Dysentery, cholera and a wound from a Song missile are all named as the cause and the sources do not agree. Kublai is a thousand miles east with the Eastern Army, which Mongke had restored to him the year before after stripping him of it. The news travels to him faster than it travels to Karakorum, and what he does with that interval decides the empire.
suggested_refs: The Diaoyucheng fortress site on Diaoyu Mountain, Hechuan, Chongqing

stops.name: Ezhou, the secret and the truce
stops.date_confidence: attested for autumn 1259; the exact date of the truce with Jia Sidao is not fixed in the reachable sources and September is inferred from the siege's course.
stops.campa: Kublai is besieging the Song fortress city of Ezhou on the Yangtze when his brother's death reaches him. He tells no one and keeps the assault going, because a claimant who is seen to break off looks like a claimant. Then he opens a private negotiation with the Song chancellor Jia Sidao, takes a promise of tribute, lifts the siege and rides north at speed. Jia Sidao will report to his own emperor that he drove the Mongols off. Both men have reasons to lie about this siege, and both do.
suggested_refs: The Ezhou negotiations of 1259 as recorded in the Song Shi and the Yuan Shi

stops.name: Kaiping, the kurultai and the crown
stops.date_confidence: attested; the kurultai proclaims him on 15 April 1260 and the formal crowning follows on 5 May. The site is Kaiping in 1260 and is only renamed Shangdu in 1264, so the common label 'crowned at Shangdu' is an anachronism.
stops.campa: At his own residence of Kaiping, Kublai convenes a kurultai of the nobles who will say yes and is proclaimed Great Khan on the fifteenth of April; on the fifth of May he is crowned. Neither assembly is held at Karakorum, and neither includes the western princes, which is precisely the objection his younger brother Ariq Boke raises within weeks at a rival kurultai of his own. In the same year Kublai issues the Jiaochao, a paper currency for the whole realm, backed by nothing but the fact that he says so.
suggested_refs: The Jiaochao paper notes of 1260, first empire-wide Mongol currency

stops.name: Karakorum, the grain cut off
stops.date_confidence: the blockade runs across 1260 to 1264 and cannot be dated to a month; January 1261 is a placeholder within that span. Karakorum changes hands more than once before Yuan forces secure it in 1264.
stops.campa: The old Mongol capital cannot feed itself. Every sack of grain that reaches it comes up from north China, and north China is Kublai's. He closes the road, and the city that Ogedei walled and Mongke ruled from begins to starve under his brother. The war between the two brothers is decided there: the brother who took the steppe's side is beaten by the brother who took the farmers' side, using the farmers. Karakorum will never be an imperial capital again.
suggested_refs: The ruins of Karakorum and the Erdene Zuu precinct built later from its stone

stops.name: Xanadu, the surrender of Ariq Boke
stops.date_confidence: attested; 21 August 1264. Kaiping is renamed Shangdu and designated summer capital in the same year, so 'Xanadu' is correct from this date forward and not before.
stops.campa: After four years Ariq Boke comes in and submits. Kublai pardons his brother and executes his brother's advisers, which is the arithmetic of a man who needs the family intact and the argument dead. The victory costs more than it settles: the western khanates have watched two grandsons of Genghis fight over a title neither could win outright, and they draw the obvious conclusion. Kublai is Great Khan of a Mongol empire that will never again act as one thing. In the same year Kaiping takes the name Shangdu.
suggested_refs: The Site of Xanadu, Zhenglan Banner, Inner Mongolia

segments.name: The City on the Taiye Lake

stops.name: Jade Island, the lake that becomes a capital
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1264; no month. Wikipedia's 'Khanbaliq' calls the Jin pleasure palace on Jade Island the Daming Palace, which is an error: the Daming Palace was the Tang complex at Chang'an. The building here was the Daning Palace.
stops.campa: Riding over the wreckage of the Jin capital, Kublai comes to a lake with an island in it, the garden the Jin emperors called the Daning Palace, and decides that the new city will be built around the water rather than the water fitted into the city. The lake becomes the Taiye; the island keeps its jade. Everything else is laid out from there on a grid by his adviser Liu Bingzhong, who had already built him Kaiping. A capital is being designed here for a man who was born in a tent.
suggested_refs: Jade Island in the Taiye Lake, now Beihai Park, Beijing

stops.name: Dadu, the walls begin
stops.date_confidence: walls from 1264, palace construction from 1274, the city complete in 1293; no month is recorded for the start and June is a placeholder within the year.
stops.campa: The walls go up on ground his grandfather emptied: genghis_khan starved the Jin capital of Zhongdu into surrender in 1215, three months before Kublai was born, and the city that stood here was burned afterwards. Kublai builds beside the ruin rather than on it. The great palace will not be started for another decade and the city will not be finished until 1293, the year before he dies. He is putting up a permanent address for a dynasty whose founder made his name by not having one.
suggested_refs: genghis_khan.journey.json, stop at Zhongdu, June 1215

stops.name: Dadu, the name Dai Yuan
stops.date_confidence: attested; 18 December 1271. Dadu is not proclaimed capital in this year, which is a common conflation; that comes in 1272.
stops.campa: By edict the Mongol regime in China takes the name Dai Yuan, the Great Origin, a phrase lifted out of the Book of Changes. It is a Chinese dynastic title for a Mongol house, and it means Kublai is claiming the Mandate rather than merely the conquest. The year before, Phagpa had presented him with a square alphabet built to write Mongol, Chinese, Tibetan and Uighur in one set of letters, and had been made Imperial Preceptor for it. A house that two years earlier had neither a script of its own nor a dynastic name now holds both by commission.
suggested_refs: Surviving 'Phags-pa script inscriptions and the paiza tablets of the Yuan

stops.name: Dadu, proclaimed the capital
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1272 per Wikipedia, 'Khanbaliq'; no month recorded. Shangdu remains the summer capital, so Dadu is the principal seat and not the only one.
stops.campa: Dadu is named the capital, and the court begins the migration it will keep for a century: winter in the walled city, summer on the steppe at Shangdu, the whole apparatus of government moving twice a year between two kinds of country. Marco Polo, who will see the winter court within four years, reports the Khan's ban on gambling among his subjects and the reason given for it, which is not a moral argument at all. The Venetian adds that he took nothing from them in practice.
stops.quote: I have conquered you by force of arms, and all that you have is mine; if, therefore, you gamble away your property, it is in fact my property that you are gambling away.
stops.quote_source: Marco Polo, The Travels, trans. Henry Yule, rev. Henri Cordier (1903), Vol. I, Book II, ch. XXXIV, on the religion and customs of the Cathayans; Project Gutenberg #10636
suggested_refs: The Yule-Cordier Travels of Marco Polo, Book II, on the ordinances of the Great Kaan

stops.name: Xiangyang, the trebuchets from Persia
stops.date_confidence: attested; the siege runs 16 October 1268 to 14 March 1273, four years and five months. Sources that call it a five-year siege are rounding.
stops.campa: The twin fortresses on the Han river hold for four years and five months, the hinge of the whole Song defence. Kublai sends to his Ilkhanid kinsmen in Persia for two Muslim engineers, Ismail and Ala al-Din, who build counterweight trebuchets of a kind China has not seen; the first stones through the roofs of Fancheng end the siege. Marco Polo will claim the machines were his family's advice, which is chronologically impossible and printed anyway. Bayan of Baarin takes command for the drive down the Yangtze.
suggested_refs: The Huihui pao counterweight trebuchets built at Xiangyang by Ismail and Ala al-Din

stops.name: Lin'an, the surrender of the child emperor
stops.date_confidence: attested for 28 March 1276 per World History Encyclopedia; the surrender is a negotiated handover of the seals rather than a storming.
stops.campa: The empress dowager Xie and the boy emperor Gong hand over the imperial seal, and the richest city on earth passes to the Yuan without a final battle. Bayan's orders are that it is not to be sacked, and it is not. The child is taken north to Kublai's court, ennobled, and eventually sent to Tibet to become a monk. Two younger Song princes are carried south by loyalists who will keep a court alive on ships for three more years, because a dynasty is easier to move than to end.
suggested_refs: The Song imperial seals surrendered at Lin'an, March 1276

stops.name: Yamen, the last fleet
stops.date_confidence: attested; 19 March 1279. Sources disagree on which Song emperor dies in the sea: Wikipedia's 'Kublai Khan' names Gong, but Gong had been taken alive in 1276; the boy drowned at Yamen is Zhao Bing, aged seven.
stops.campa: The last Song fleet is chained together in the estuary off Yamen and broken by Yuan ships in a day. The minister Lu Xiufu straps the imperial seal to his back, takes the seven-year-old emperor Zhao Bing in his arms and walks off the deck into the water; the histories say a hundred thousand followed them over the side. Kublai now rules all of China, the first ruler from the steppe ever to do so. He governs it from a city he built himself, under a dynastic name he chose.
suggested_refs: The Yamen memorial cliff at the mouth of the Xi river, Guangdong

stops.name: Khanbaliq, the hundred learned men
stops.date_confidence: the marco_polo journey places Niccolo and Maffeo before the Great Khan in 1266 with the golden tablet; the month is not fixed. The speech itself survives only in Ramusio's sixteenth-century recension, not in the older manuscript tradition.
stops.campa: Niccolo and Maffeo Polo, merchants who came east for profit and found themselves at the far end of the world, are received at Kublai's court and sent home with a golden tablet of safe conduct and an errand: bring back a hundred men learned in the Christian law, and oil from the lamp at the Holy Sepulchre. The atlas carries them here in marco_polo. The Pope never sends the hundred men. What comes back instead, nine years later, is one of their sons.
stops.quote: How would you have me to become a Christian? You see that the Christians of these parts are so ignorant that they achieve nothing and can achieve nothing, whilst you see the Idolaters can do anything they please... But now you shall go to your Pope, and pray him on my part to send hither an hundred men skilled in your law... When we shall witness this we will denounce the Idolaters and their religion, and then I will receive baptism.
stops.quote_source: Marco Polo, The Travels, trans. Henry Yule, rev. Henri Cordier (1903), Vol. I, Book II, ch. VI, Note 1, quoting Ramusio's addition; Project Gutenberg #10636
suggested_refs: Ramusio's 1559 Venice recension, source of the hundred-learned-men speech

stops.name: Shangdu, Marco Polo received at the summer court
stops.date_confidence: the marco_polo journey dates the arrival at the summer court to 1 May 1275. Wikipedia gives Polo seventeen years of service and World History Encyclopedia gives 1275 to 1292; the start year is not firmly fixed and no Chinese source names him.
stops.campa: The brothers come back, and this time there are three of them. They find the Khan at his summer palace of marble and bamboo on the steppe, and Niccolo presents the young man beside him as his son and the Khan's liegeman. Kublai's answer is four words. Marco is twenty-one, has been three and a half years on the road, and will not see Venice again for seventeen years. The atlas carries him here as marco_polo; nothing in the Yuan archives carries him anywhere at all.
stops.quote_source: Marco Polo, The Travels, trans. Henry Yule, rev. Henri Cordier (1903), Vol. I, Prologue, ch. XIV, on the presentation of the Polos to the Great Kaan; Project Gutenberg #10636
suggested_refs: The Site of Xanadu summer palace precinct, Zhenglan Banner

stops.name: Khanbaliq, the young Venetian taken into service
stops.date_confidence: the marco_polo journey dates entry into the Khan's service to 1 September 1275. The Travels give the substance of Kublai's standing complaint about envoys without naming a date.
stops.campa: Kublai takes the young Venetian into his service and sends him out on missions across the empire. Polo notices early what his master actually wants from a returning envoy, and it is not the business he was sent on. The Khan collects countries the way other rulers collect tribute: through the mouths of men who have been there. It is the same appetite that brought Haiyun to his tent at Karakorum thirty years before, and it is why the book that made Europe imagine Asia exists at all.
stops.quote: I had far liever hearken about the strange things, and the manners of the different countries you have seen, than merely be told of the business you went upon.
stops.quote_source: Marco Polo, The Travels, trans. Henry Yule, rev. Henri Cordier (1903), Vol. I, Prologue, ch. XV, on why Mark took pains to observe foreign lands; Project Gutenberg #10636
suggested_refs: The Yule-Cordier Travels, Prologue chapters on Marco's embassies

stops.name: Yangzhou, the governorship no Chinese record confirms
stops.date_confidence: traditional and disputed. The marco_polo journey carries the three-year governorship at 1279; other readings place it about 1282 to 1285. No Yuan Shi entry and no local gazetteer names Polo as governor, and the claim is widely doubted.
stops.campa: Marco Polo says that Kublai made him governor of Yangzhou on the Grand Canal for three years. No Chinese record says so, and the office he describes does not match any post the Yuan actually had in the city. Historians have been picking at this claim for two centuries without settling it: an exaggeration by a salt commissioner, a copyist's inflation, or a plain fact that fell out of the archives. The atlas keeps the stop in marco_polo and keeps the doubt with it.
suggested_refs: The Yangzhou governorship claim in The Travels, unconfirmed by any Yuan source

stops.name: Khanbaliq, the minister Ahmad
stops.date_confidence: undated in the verified pool. The Travels give the exchange without a year, and the placement at 1280 is editorial, sitting inside the period of Ahmad Fanakati's financial ascendancy at court.
stops.campa: Ahmad Fanakati runs the Khan's finances and, by Polo's account, runs his own accounts through them. When the minister wants a man dead he comes to Kublai and says that such an one deserves death, for he hath done this or that against your imperial dignity. The Khan's answer is the same every time, and the men are executed. Polo records the words as a warning about trust rather than about cruelty. The Great Khan whose own administrators were once audited down to a hundred and forty-two breaches no longer checks the man nearest him.
stops.quote_source: Marco Polo, The Travels, trans. Henry Yule, rev. Henri Cordier (1903), Vol. I, Book II, on the minister Ahmad Fanakati; Project Gutenberg #10636
suggested_refs: The Yule-Cordier Travels, Book II, chapters on Ahmad Fanakati's ministry

stops.name: Karajang, the envoy sent west
stops.date_confidence: the marco_polo journey dates the Karajang mission to 1283; no month. The mission rests on Polo's own testimony alone.
stops.campa: Kublai sends the Venetian to Karajang, the province the Mongols made out of the Dali kingdom Kublai himself took thirty years earlier. Polo comes back with the account that gives Europe its first description of Yunnan: the crocodiles he calls serpents, the gold traded by weight against silver, the salt-money, the tattooed men. He is travelling on Yuan roads through a country that exists as a province because his master crossed a river on inflated hides in 1253. The atlas carries the stop in marco_polo.
suggested_refs: The Karajang chapters of The Travels, first European account of Yunnan

stops.name: Zaiton, the Lady Kokotchin sails
stops.date_confidence: the marco_polo journey dates the departure from Zaiton to March 1291; the fleet reaches Hormuz in 1293 and the Polos learn there that Arghun has died.
stops.campa: A Mongol princess of seventeen is to be sent by sea to marry the Ilkhan Arghun in Persia, and the Polos get their release by escorting her. Fourteen ships leave the harbour the Arabs call Zaiton. The marriage embassy is Kublai's, arranged between two branches of a family that no longer obeys one khan but still exchanges brides. By the time the fleet reaches Hormuz, Arghun is dead. The atlas carries marco_polo out of China here, and the old Khan will die three years later without seeing any of them again.
suggested_refs: The port of Zaiton, Quanzhou, Fujian, terminus of the maritime silk route

stops.name: Khanbaliq, the letter to the King of Japan
stops.date_confidence: attested to the eighth month of 1266; the day is not given. The Classical Chinese original is preserved at Todai-ji in Nara. Only the opening and closing lines of the letter were read directly in this research; the body is taken on the translator's authority.
stops.campa: Kublai writes to Japan. The letter opens with the Mandate of Heaven and closes by leaving the matter to Your Highness's careful consideration, and in between it notes that Korea has already submitted and observes that nobody wants to resort to arms. The Kamakura shogunate does not answer it, or the five embassies that follow. The document survives at Todai-ji in Nara, kept by the country that refused it, which is the only reason anyone can still read what the Great Khan was willing to say before he sent ships.
stops.quote: The Emperor of the Great Mongols, being commissioned by Heaven, hereby respectfully presents a letter to the King of Japan.
stops.quote_source: Letter of Kublai Khan to the King of Japan, eighth month of 1266, original preserved at Todai-ji, Nara; quoted in Stephen Turnbull, The Mongol Invasions of Japan 1274 and 1281 (Osprey, 2010), p. 14
suggested_refs: The 1266 letter of Kublai Khan preserved at Todai-ji, Nara
sources: Stephen Turnbull, The Mongol Invasions of Japan 1274 and 1281 (2010)

stops.name: Komoda Beach, the first landing
stops.date_confidence: attested; 4 November 1274 by the standard reckoning of the Hachiman Gudokun narrative.
stops.campa: The fleet makes its first landfall of the Japan campaign on the beach at Komoda on Tsushima. The deputy shugo So Sukekuni rides down to the shore with eighty horsemen against an army, and is killed with all of them. The island is overrun in a day. Japanese accounts of what follows on Tsushima and Iki are the reason the invasion is remembered in Japan as an atrocity rather than a campaign, and the reason the second fleet, seven years later, will find every likely landing beach walled.
suggested_refs: The Komoda beach memorial to So Sukekuni, Tsushima

stops.name: Hakata Bay, the fleet withdraws
stops.date_confidence: attested for 19 and 20 November 1274. Whether the storm that wrecked the fleet or the decision to re-embark came first is not settled by the sources.
stops.campa: Some nine hundred ships put a Mongol, Chinese and Korean army ashore near Hakata a day after taking Iki. The samurai fight in the manner they know, single challenges against massed archery and exploding shot, and are pushed back to the old fortifications inland. Then the invaders go back to their ships for the night, and a storm off the coast breaks the fleet on the rocks. The Japanese will not call it a divine wind until after the second one. From here they start building a wall.
suggested_refs: The Genko Borui defensive wall raised along Hakata Bay after 1274

stops.name: Hakata Bay, the second armada
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the pool gives no day for the main disaster and August is the standard placing of the typhoon. The diversionary attack of three hundred ships on the Nagato coast is firmly dated 25 June 1281.
stops.campa: Two fleets, an eastern route army out of Korea and a southern out of the conquered Song ports, together some hundred and forty thousand men, converge on Kyushu. Three hundred ships strike the Nagato coast in June as a diversion and are driven off. The main force cannot get past the stone wall at Hakata and sits at anchor off Takashima through the summer, chained together against fireships, until a typhoon comes down on it. The largest seaborne invasion attempted anywhere before the twentieth century ends on the rocks.
suggested_refs: The Takashima underwater excavation site, wrecks of the 1281 fleet

stops.name: Cha Ban, the burning of Vijaya
stops.date_confidence: the invasion of Champa is launched in 1282 and Sogetu takes the sacked capital in early 1283; the pool supports 1282 to 1283 and the month within 1283 is not fixed.
stops.campa: Champa refuses tribute, and Kublai sends a fleet under Sogetu against it. The Cham burn their own capital and go into the hills, and the Mongols occupy a city that is already ash. King Indravarman V, who is over eighty, conducts the rest of the war from the mountains and never once offers battle. Sogetu will be killed two years later in Dai Viet, on the far side of the same campaign. The Yuan hold the coast of Champa and control nothing behind it.
suggested_refs: The Cha Ban citadel ruins near Quy Nhon, Binh Dinh province

stops.name: Thang Long, the third invasion
stops.date_confidence: the third invasion is launched in 1287 and withdraws in 1288; no month is given in the pool for the launch. The second invasion of 1285 also takes and loses the capital before tributary relations are agreed.
stops.campa: For the third time a Yuan army comes down the Red River, and for the third time the capital is taken and turns out to be worth nothing. Tran Hung Dao lets the country go and takes the supply fleet instead, planting iron-tipped stakes in the bed of the Bach Dang at low water. The retreating ships come down on the falling tide onto the stakes. Dai Viet then sends tribute to Dadu and Kublai accepts it, so one court records a submission and the other records a victory.
suggested_refs: The Bach Dang stake field, excavated at Quang Yen, Quang Ninh
sources: Dai Viet Su Ky Toan Thu

stops.name: Pagan, the sack that may not have happened
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Yuan Shi and Marco Polo both report the capture of Pagan in 1287; Michael Aung-Thwin argues the Mongol column halted some 160 kilometres short of the city. No month is fixed and June is a placeholder.
stops.campa: The Yuan court's annals say the army took Pagan and ended the kingdom, and Marco Polo, who was not there either, says the same. Modern scholarship says the column stopped a hundred miles north and that the Burmese kingdom fell apart on its own, from a succession murder and the loss of its tax base. Both stories end with Pagan finished; they disagree about whose hand did it. The atlas keeps both, because the temples on the plain are standing either way and the kingdom is not.
suggested_refs: The Bagan temple plain, Mandalay Region, Myanmar
sources: Michael Aung-Thwin, cited in Wikipedia, 'First Mongol invasion of Burma'

stops.name: Zaiton, the fleet for Java
stops.date_confidence: Kublai issues the order to subdue Java in March 1292 and the fleet sails from Quanzhou late that year, reaching Java in January 1293. The often-cited '1292-01' predates the order itself.
stops.campa: A Javanese king branded a Yuan envoy in the face, and Kublai, seventy-seven years old, orders a fleet across the ocean about it. By the time it arrives Kertanagara is already dead and his kingdom swallowed by a rival, so the Mongols fight the wrong enemy in alliance with a prince named Raden Wijaya, who then turns on them and drives them to their ships. The losses are given as three thousand in one summary and as twelve to eighteen thousand, about sixty per cent of the force, in the fuller account. Wijaya founds Majapahit.
suggested_refs: The Quanzhou maritime museum's Yuan-era hull, raised from the harbour mud

stops.name: Dadu, the death of Chabi
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month recorded. Her son and Kublai's designated heir Zhenjin dies on 5 January 1286, five years later.
stops.campa: Chabi dies. She had been his chief empress for forty-seven years, had argued him out of turning north China into pasture, had intervened for the captured Song imperial family, and had designed a riding coat for him that the Yuan court then wore. Zhenjin, the heir Haiyun named, dies five years after her. Kublai marries Nambui in 1283 and does not replace either of them. The witnesses who told him no are gone, and the last decade of the reign is the decade after they stopped.
suggested_refs: The Yuan imperial portrait album images of Chabi Khatun

stops.name: Dadu, Sangha and the new paper money
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1287; Wikipedia's 'Kublai Khan' states the Zhiyuan Chao was created in 1287 to deal with a budget shortfall. Sources that date it 1286 are a year early. No month.
stops.campa: The wars have emptied the treasury: two fleets lost off Japan, three campaigns in Vietnam, an army in Burma. Kublai's fiscal chief Sangha, a Tibetan raised under Phagpa's patronage, issues a second paper currency, the Zhiyuan Chao, to cover the shortfall, and the notes of 1260 begin their long slide. In the same years the Drikung Kagyu rise in Tibet against Yuan-backed Sakya authority, and in 1291 Kublai's grandson Buqa-Temur puts the revolt down at a reported cost of ten thousand lives.
suggested_refs: Surviving Zhiyuan Chao notes and printing blocks of the later Yuan

stops.name: Dadu, the Khan dies in his winter palace
stops.date_confidence: attested; 18 February 1294. He is seventy-eight, born 23 September 1215. Wikipedia gives seventy-eight and World History Encyclopedia gives seventy-nine to eighty; the arithmetic supports seventy-eight.
stops.campa: Kublai dies in Dadu at seventy-eight, gouty, obese and drinking, in the city he finished building the year before. He is the only one of Genghis Khan's successors to rule from a permanent capital of his own making rather than a moving camp, and the western khanates have long since stopped taking his orders. His grandson Temur is enthroned after him, chosen with Zhenjin's widow behind the choice. The Yuan will hold China for seventy-four more years and then go back north to the grass.
suggested_refs: The Yuan Shi annals of the Shizu reign, closing entries

stops.name: Ikh Khorig, the unmarked ground
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Yuan Shi records only that the body was sent north for burial and names no site. Interment near Burkhan Khaldun follows the Genghisid pattern and the Great Taboo of the guarded precinct, but no tomb has been found. The month is unrecorded.
stops.campa: The body goes north out of the capital he built, back to the country he spent his reign not living in, and into the guarded ground the Mongols call the Great Taboo. The Yuan Shi says only that he was sent north. Riders are said to have trampled the grave flat and horses driven over it until nothing showed. Genghis Khan lies somewhere in the same precinct on the same terms. The Khan who invented an address for the dynasty is buried at no address at all, and has never been found.
suggested_refs: The Ikh Khorig precinct below Burkhan Khaldun, Khentii, closed for centuries

stops.name: Miaoying Temple, the white stupa and the portrait
stops.date_confidence: the White Stupa at Miaoying Temple is dated 1279; the posthumous portrait is drawn in 1294. The White Dagoba in Beihai Park is a different structure, built in 1651 under the Qing, and the two are routinely confused.
stops.campa: Araniko, a Newar artist brought from Nepal at twenty-two to cast and build for the Yuan, raises a white Tibetan-style stupa in the western quarter of Dadu, the tallest thing in the capital. Fifteen years later, with Kublai dead, he draws the portrait that becomes the official face: heavy, white-bearded, in white robes, the gaze turned aside. Every later image of Kublai Khan descends from that one sitting, and the stupa still stands where he put it while the palace it overlooked is gone.
suggested_refs: The White Stupa of Miaoying Temple, Beijing, and the Yuan imperial portrait albums

stops.name: Genoa, the book dictated in prison
stops.date_confidence: composition is dated to about 1298 to 1299, in Genoese captivity; the month is unknown. No autograph survives and the original language is Franco-Venetian.
stops.campa: Four years after Kublai's death, a Venetian prisoner of war dictates his Asia to a cellmate who writes romances for a living. The original manuscript is lost. About a hundred and fifty copies survive in six textual traditions, no two agreeing; Pipino turns it into Latin by 1302, Ramusio collates a version at Venice in 1559, Frampton puts it into English in 1579 from a Spanish text. Everything Europe thinks it knows about the Great Khan comes through this book, and the book comes through a copyist's chain nobody can untangle.
suggested_refs: The six manuscript traditions of the Travels grouped by Philippe Menard

stops.name: Shangdu, the ruins on the steppe
stops.date_confidence: the sack by Ming forces is dated 1369; the month is not recorded. Stephen Bushell documents the surviving ruins in 1872, Chinese preservation work begins in 2002, and UNESCO inscribes the site in 2012.
stops.campa: Ming armies burn the summer capital in the year after the Yuan lose China, and the court that flees north never comes back to it. Five centuries later the British diplomat Stephen Bushell walks over the site and finds temple foundations, marble blocks and roof tiles lying in the grass. UNESCO inscribes it in 2012 as the place where two ways of building a city, the steppe camp and the Chinese grid, were once made to share a wall. What is left of the pleasure dome is a rectangle of turf.
suggested_refs: The Site of Xanadu, UNESCO World Heritage inscription of 2012

stops.name: Beijing, the city under other dynasties
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction of a geographic echo, not a meeting. The date is the arrival of Matteo Ricci at Beijing carried by the matteo_ricci journey; Mao Zedong's clerkship at Peking University is dated September 1918 in the mao_zedong journey.
stops.campa: The Jesuit matteo_ricci is received at the Ming court in the city Kublai laid out, three hundred and twenty-five years after the walls went up, and the Ming have kept the grid while renaming everything on it. Three centuries after that, mao_zedong sorts newspapers in a library a few streets from the same lake. Nobody meets Kublai here. The plan holds under all of them: the Taiye water, the axis, the position of the gates. He built the one thing in the empire that outlasted the empire.
suggested_refs: matteo_ricci.journey.json, Beijing, 24 January 1601; mao_zedong.journey.json, Beijing, September 1918

stops.name: Ash Farm, the dream of Xanadu
stops.date_confidence: contested. The Crewe manuscript says autumn 1797, Coleridge's printed preface says summer 1797, and some scholars argue May 1798. The opium dream and the person from Porlock come from Coleridge's own preface and are generally read as a literary frame rather than as an account of events.
stops.campa: In a farmhouse on Exmoor an English poet falls asleep over a sentence in Purchas his Pilgrimes about a wall enclosing sixteen miles of meadow, and wakes with two or three hundred lines in his head. He gets fifty-four down before a man from Porlock knocks. In Xanadu did Kubla Khan a stately pleasure-dome decree: a Mongol emperor's summer camp, filtered through a Venetian, an English compiler and an opium doze, and left unfinished. He keeps the poem in a drawer for nineteen years until Byron makes him print it.
suggested_refs: The Crewe manuscript of 'Kubla Khan', British Library
